title: Testing TypeScript Applications
learning_outcomes: Explain unit, integration, and end-to-end testing in the context of testing typescript applications.
Apply the lesson concept in a small TypeScript example and describe what the compiler can check.
Identify one limitation or failure case and choose an appropriate runtime check or test when needed.

content.intro: Learn testing typescript applications through a compact mental model, syllabus-aligned subtopics, a worked example and a practical task. The goal is not to memorize syntax but to know what the type contract guarantees and what evidence is still needed.
content.why_it_matters: Professional TypeScript code needs repeatable tests, clear public contracts, and explicit failure behavior. Keep abstractions proportional to the problem and test both values and inferred type relationships.

content_blocks.title: Mental model
content_blocks.text: **Testing TypeScript Applications.** This lesson belongs to **Testing and Quality Assurance**. Start by identifying the problem that testing typescript applications solves. In TypeScript, separate three questions: what values your program intends to accept, what the compiler can prove from the code, and what must still be checked while the program runs. The last category matters whenever data comes from a user, file, API, storage layer, or an untyped JavaScript dependency.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus topics and how to use them

items.title: Unit, integration, and end-to-end testing
items.text: For unit, integration, and end-to-end testing, define observable acceptance criteria and test both expected behavior and a failure case. Preserve a small regression test for any bug or inference problem you fix.

items.title: Test environment setup
items.text: For test environment setup, treat incoming values as untrusted until runtime checks establish the required shape. A TypeScript annotation does not validate network, file, database, storage, or user-provided data by itself.

items.title: Maintaining testable code
items.text: For maintaining testable code, define observable acceptance criteria and test both expected behavior and a failure case. Preserve a small regression test for any bug or inference problem you fix.

This test example expects Vitest in a local disposable project; install it with `npm install --save-dev vitest` and run `npx vitest run` after saving the example as a test file. content_blocks.title: Compile-time versus runtime
content_blocks.text: Type annotations and most type declarations are erased when TypeScript emits JavaScript. They do not validate external JSON, authorize a user, sanitize HTML, or prevent runtime failures by themselves. Validate trust-boundary inputs and test the behavior.

content.task: Create a small TypeScript example for “Testing TypeScript Applications”. Demonstrate unit, integration, and end-to-end testing, explain your assumption, and include one check that shows the expected behavior. Do not treat a type annotation as runtime validation for external input.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates at least one syllabus subtopic named in this lesson.
The type contract is explicit enough that another learner can explain what it accepts and rejects.
The learner records a failure case and distinguishes compile-time checks from runtime validation.
hints: Start with the syllabus item “Unit, integration, and end-to-end testing” and define the smallest example that demonstrates it.
Ask which part is checked by TypeScript and which part depends on runtime data, the environment or a test.
For external input, start with unknown and validate the required shape before using a domain type.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating a successful type check as a runtime guarantee.
common_mistakes.why: Type annotations do not generally validate data after JavaScript starts running.
common_mistakes.fix: Add runtime checks for external input and tests for meaningful failure cases.

common_mistakes.problem: Using any or an assertion to silence a useful diagnostic.
common_mistakes.why: That can hide the exact mismatch the type system would otherwise report.
common_mistakes.fix: Prefer a more precise type or unknown plus narrowing; use assertions only when a verified invariant justifies them.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a compiler setting or runtime example without checking the project environment.
common_mistakes.why: Module resolution, DOM/Node globals, JSX and tool behavior depend on the configured versions and environment.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin the toolchain, match tsconfig to the runtime/bundler, and run the actual project's typecheck and tests.

summary: Testing TypeScript Applications is taught through the subtopics listed in the source syllabus: Unit, integration, and end-to-end testing, Test environment setup, Maintaining testable code.
Prefer precise contracts and use compiler diagnostics as evidence, not as a replacement for runtime tests.
Validate untrusted data and describe environment/version assumptions explicitly.
